evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 2D classification data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Complex III and CIV subunits were identified in the mixed mitochondrial pooled fraction by mass spectrometry.
source: Complex III and CIV subunits were identified in the mixed mitochondrial pooled fraction by mass spectrometry, in addition to CI subunits (Supplementary file 1a, see Materials and methods for full dataset availability).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: This is an example of 'bottom-up structural proteomics' on a partially purified sample.
source: This is an example of 'bottom-up structural proteomics' (Ho et al., 2020) on a partially purified sample, in which a single sample was used for the structural determination of multiple respiratory complexes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation.

claim: Processing of the CIII2 and SC III2+IV particles resulted in near-atomic reconstructions of CIII2 at 3.2 Å, of CIV at 3.8 Å and of SC III2+IV at 3.8 Å.
source: Processing of the CIII2 and SC III2+IV particles resulted in near-atomic reconstructions of CIII2 at 3.2 Å, of CIV at 3.8 Å and of SC III2+IV at 3.8 Å (Figure 1, Videos 1–3, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3, Table 1, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 1, Table 1, and supplementary materials.

claim: Pooled fractions of the preparation contained CIII2 respiratory activity (electron transfer from reduced decylubiquinone to cytochrome c) that was inhibited by CIII2 inhibitors antimycin A and myxothiazol.
source: Further examination using spectroscopic activity assays (Belt et al., 2017) confirmed that pooled fractions of the preparation contained CIII2 respiratory activity (electron transfer from reduced decylubiquinone to cytochrome c) that was inhibited by CIII2 inhibitors antimycin A and myxothiazol (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by activity assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The sample showed CIV activity from reduced cytochrome c to oxygen that was inhibited by CIV inhibitor potassium cyanide.
source: The sample also showed CIV activity from reduced cytochrome c to oxygen that was inhibited by CIV inhibitor potassium cyanide (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by activity assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: MPP activity of CIII2 was recovered from isolated V. radiata mitochondrial membranes.
source: Although MPP activity of CIII2 was recovered from isolated V. radiata mitochondrial membranes (not shown), MPP activity assays (Braun et al., 1992; Teixeira et al., 2015) of the pooled fractions were inconclusive.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: MPP activity assays of the pooled fractions were inconclusive.
source: Although MPP activity of CIII2 was recovered from isolated V. radiata mitochondrial membranes (not shown), MPP activity assays (Braun et al., 1992; Teixeira et al., 2015) of the pooled fractions were inconclusive.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The high superposition between the V. radiata MPP domain and structures of active MPP supports the interpretation that the inability to confirm MPP activity does not significantly impact data interpretation.
source: However, given the high superposition between the V. radiata MPP domain shown here and structures of active MPP (see below), we believe our inability to confirm MPP activity in this case does not significantly impact our interpretation of the data.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons in Figure 3.

claim: VrCIII2 contains 10 subunits per CIII monomer (three conserved, mitochondrially encoded subunits and seven accessory subunits).
source: The V. radiata (Vr) structure confirms that VrCIII2 contains 10 subunits per CIII monomer (three conserved, mitochondrially encoded subunits and seven accessory subunits), similar to yeast and mammals (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 2.

claim: VrCIII2 contains 13 transmembrane helices per protomer.
source: As in mammals and yeast, VrCIII2 contains 13 transmembrane helices per protomer: eight from COB (cyt b) and one from each of CYC1 (cyt c1), UCR1, QCR8, QCR9, and QCR10 (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The MPP domain, composed of two MPP-α/β heterodimers (one per CIII protomer), extends into the matrix.
source: The MPP domain, composed of two MPP-α/β heterodimers (one per CIII protomer), extends into the matrix.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 2.

claim: The C-terminus of CYC1 (six α-helices and a 2-strand β-sheet), the entire QCR6 subunit and UCR1's head domain extend into the intermembrane space (IMS).
source: The C-terminus of CYC1 (six α-helices and a 2-strand β-sheet), the entire QCR6 subunit and UCR1's head domain extend into the intermembrane space (IMS).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 2.

claim: The linker and head domains of UCR1 (Rieske iron-sulfur subunit) were disordered in the reconstruction and an atomic model was not produced for this region of UCR1.
source: Consistent with their known flexibility and conformational heterogeneity, the linker and head domains of UCR1 (Rieske iron-sulfur subunit) were disordered in our reconstruction and an atomic model was not produced for this region of UCR1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: All heme groups (heme bH, bL and heme c1) were clearly visible and modelled into each cyt b and cyt c1 subunit of the dimer.
source: All heme groups (heme bH, bL and heme c1) were clearly visible and modelled into each cyt b and cyt c1 subunit of the dimer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 2B.

claim: The distances between the hemes were consistent with that previously seen in other organisms.
source: The distances between the hemes were consistent with that previously seen in other organisms (Figure 2B and C; Cramer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 2C and citation.

claim: A catalytic Zn2+ ion was visible and modelled into each MPP-β subunit.
source: A catalytic Zn2+ ion was also visible and modelled into each MPP-β subunit (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 2B.

claim: The iron-sulfur clusters were not modeled due to the inability to build an atomic model for the head domain of UCR1.
source: Given that we were not able to build an atomic model for the head domain of UCR1, we did not model the iron-sulfur clusters (see 3DVA analysis below for more details).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Density consistent with cardiolipin, phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylcholine lipids was found and modelled into the VrCIII2 map.
source: Density consistent with cardiolipin, phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylcholine lipids was found and modelled into the VrCIII2 map (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 2E.

claim: Similar to yeast, the CIII2 lipids concentrate in lipophilic cavities in COB, CYC1, UCR1, QCR8 and QCR10 close to the QN site.
source: Similar to that previously seen in yeast, the CIII2 lipids concentrate in lipophilic cavities in COB, CYC1, UCR1, QCR8 and QCR10 close to the QN site, both on the surface of CIII2 and at the interface between the CIII protomers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 2E.

claim: Additional lipids were observed on the exterior of COB close to the QP site.
source: We also observed additional lipids on the exterior of COB close to the QP site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 2E.

claim: The vast majority of the residues that form the QP and QN sites and inhibitor-binding pockets in yeast and bovine CIII2 are conserved in V. radiata.
source: The vast majority of the residues that form the QP and QN sites and inhibitor-binding pockets in yeast and bovine CIII2 (Xia et al., 2013; Esser et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2003) are conserved in V. radiata (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence alignment in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citations.

claim: The COB residues that form H-bonds with ubiquinone at the QN site of yeast and bovine CIII2 are conserved in V. radiata (His208, Ser212, D235).
source: In particular, the COB residues that have been shown to form H-bonds with ubiquinone at the QN site of yeast and bovine CIII2 are conserved in V. radiata (His208, Ser212, D235), as are the key residues of COB's cd1 helix (Gly149-Ile253) and the PEWY motif (Pro277-Tyr280).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence alignment in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The key residues of COB's cd1 helix (Gly149-Ile253) and the PEWY motif (Pro277-Tyr280) are conserved in V. radiata.
source: In particular, the COB residues that have been shown to form H-bonds with ubiquinone at the QN site of yeast and bovine CIII2 are conserved in V. radiata (His208, Ser212, D235), as are the key residues of COB's cd1 helix (Gly149-Ile253) and the PEWY motif (Pro277-Tyr280).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence alignment in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: No clear density for endogenous quinone was visible in any of the binding sites of the V. radiata dimer.
source: Nevertheless, no clear density for endogenous quinone was visible in any of the binding sites of the V. radiata dimer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The mRNAs of several subunits of plant respiratory complexes undergo cytidine-to-uridine RNA editing at several sites.
source: It is well established that the mRNAs of several subunits of plant respiratory complexes, including several CI subunits, CIII's COB and CIV's COX1-3, undergo cytidine-to-uridine RNA editing at several sites (Covello and Gray, 1989; Gualberto et al., 1989; Hiesel et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Mitochondrial RNA editing is widely conserved across vascular and non-vascular plants.
source: This mitochondrial RNA editing is widely conserved across vascular and non-vascular plants (Takenaka et al., 2013; Sper-Whitis et al., 1996), and most generally acts to restore consensus conserved sequences (Small et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: RNA editing most generally acts to restore consensus conserved sequences.
source: This mitochondrial RNA editing is widely conserved across vascular and non-vascular plants (Takenaka et al., 2013; Sper-Whitis et al., 1996), and most generally acts to restore consensus conserved sequences (Small et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: The A. thaliana COB RNA-editing sites are conserved in V. radiata.
source: Inspection of the cryoEM density for the VrCOB subunits showed that the A. thaliana COB RNA-editing sites (Bentolila et al., 2008; Giegé and Brennicke, 1999) are conserved in V. radiata.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data and citations.

claim: V. radiata COB contains additional RNA edit sites present in wheat, potato and rice.
source: Moreover, V. radiata COB contains additional RNA edit sites present in wheat, potato and rice (Ito et al., 1996; Zanlungo et al., 1993; Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations and supplementary data.

claim: Residues were mutated to the edited residues in the model based on conservation pattern and unambiguous cryoEM density.
source: Given the conservation pattern and the fact that the cryoEM density at these sites was unambiguous, residues were mutated to the edited residues in our model.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing model building decisions.

claim: RNA editing was identified in V. radiata's COX1 and 3.
source: RNA editing was also identified in V. radiata's COX1 and 3 (see CIV section), as well as in CI subunits (Maldonado et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Supplementary file 1d.

claim: The sequence conservation of V. radiata mitochondrially encoded CIII2 subunits (COB, CYC1, UCR1) with respect to S. cerevisiae and bovine homologs is modest (~50%).
source: Although the sequence conservation of the V. radiata (Vr) mitochondrially encoded CIII2 subunits (COB, CYC1, UCR1) with respect to Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Sc) and bovine (Bos taurus, Bt) homologs is modest (~50%), their structural conservation is high (0.75–0.95 Å main chain RMSD, Figure 2—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence and structural comparisons in Figure 2—figure supplements 2–3.

claim: The structural conservation of V. radiata mitochondrially encoded CIII2 subunits with respect to S. cerevisiae and bovine homologs is high (0.75–0.95 Å main chain RMSD).
source: Although the sequence conservation of the V. radiata (Vr) mitochondrially encoded CIII2 subunits (COB, CYC1, UCR1) with respect to Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Sc) and bovine (Bos taurus, Bt) homologs is modest (~50%), their structural conservation is high (0.75–0.95 Å main chain RMSD, Figure 2—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons in Figure 2—figure supplements 2–3.

claim: VrUCR1 shows an extended N-terminal unstructured loop and short helix that provide more extensive contacts with MPP-β.
source: Whereas the helix is highly structurally conserved, VrUCR1 shows an extended N-terminal unstructured loop and short helix that provide more extensive contacts with MPP-β (see MPP section below).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: VrQCR7 is missing an N-terminal helix that in yeast provides several additional contacts with cyt b's helix H and FG loop.
source: Nevertheless, similar to the bovine homolog, VrQCR7 is missing an N-terminal helix that in yeast provides several additional contacts with cyt b's helix H and FG loop (Figure 2—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons in Figure 2—figure supplement 3H.

claim: VrQCR8 lacks a short perpendicular helix that stacks below cyt b's helix H in yeast.
source: Nevertheless, like BtUQCRQ but in contrast to ScQcr8, VrQCR8 lacks a short perpendicular helix that stacks below cyt b's helix H in yeast (Figure 2—figure supplement 3I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons in Figure 2—figure supplement 3I.

claim: ScQcr8 has a longer unstructured N-terminus that extends into the cavity of the MPP domain, contacting helix a and DE loop of COB in the same CIII protomer, as well as the helix a of COB of the opposite protomer.
source: Moreover, ScQcr8 also has a longer unstructured N-terminus that extends into the cavity of the MPP domain, contacting helix a and DE loop of COB in the same CIII protomer, as well as the helix a of COB of the opposite protomer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons.

claim: The interaction interface between VrQCR8 and VrCOB is reduced relative to that of yeast.
source: Therefore, the interaction interface between VrQCR8 and VrCOB is reduced relative to that of yeast (Figure 2—figure supplement 3J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons in Figure 2—figure supplement 3J.

claim: The VrMPP-α/β dimer shows the overall 'clam shell' configuration.
source: The VrMPP-α/β dimer shows this overall 'clam shell' configuration, with a highly negative surface in the interior of the cavity (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The interior cavity of VrMPP-α/β has a highly negative surface.
source: The VrMPP-α/β dimer shows this overall 'clam shell' configuration, with a highly negative surface in the interior of the cavity (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrostatic potential data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The negative surface of the MPP cavity has been shown to interact with the generally positively charged pre-sequences of the MPP substrates.
source: This negative surface has been shown to interact with the generally positively charged pre-sequences of the MPP substrates (Taylor et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation.

claim: VrMPP-β contains the characteristic inverse Zn-binding HxxEH motif of pitrilysin endopeptidases.
source: VrMPP-β contains the characteristic inverse Zn-binding HxxEH motif of pitrilysin endopeptidases, as well as all the conserved catalytic residues (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Gakh et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 3B and citation.

claim: VrMPP-β contains all the conserved catalytic residues.
source: VrMPP-β contains the characteristic inverse Zn-binding HxxEH motif of pitrilysin endopeptidases, as well as all the conserved catalytic residues (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Gakh et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 3B and citation.

claim: The cryoEM map shows density for the Zn2+ ion, which is coordinated by residues His137, His141, Glu217.
source: Our cryoEM map shows density for the Zn2+ ion, which is coordinated by residues His137, His141, Glu217 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 3B.

claim: The fourth Zn2+-coordinating atom—the oxygen of the water molecule that exerts the nucleophilic attack on the carbonyl carbon of the peptide bond—was not modelled.
source: The fourth Zn2+-coordinating atom—the oxygen of the water molecule that exerts the nucleophilic attack on the carbonyl carbon of the peptide bond (Gakh et al., 2002)—was not modelled.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The glutamate that acts as a general base catalyst of the water molecule (Glu140) is conserved in V. radiata.
source: The glutamate that acts as a general base catalyst of this water molecule (Gakh et al., 2002; Taylor et al., 2001) (Glu140) is also conserved in V. radiata.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 3B and citations.

claim: MPP-β residues confirmed in the substrate-bound yeast soluble MPP structure to be critical for substrate recognition are conserved in VrMPP-β (Glu227, Asp231, Phe144, Asn167, Ala168, Tyr169).
source: MPP-β residues that were confirmed in the substrate-bound yeast soluble MPP structure (Taylor et al., 2001) to be critical for substrate recognition are conserved both in the sequence and structural location in VrMPP-β (Glu227, Asp231, Phe144, Asn167, Ala168, Tyr169; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 3B and citation.

claim: VrMPP-α contains the flexible glycine-rich stretch believed to be involved in substrate binding and/or product release in soluble ScMPP-α.
source: Additionally, VrMPP-α contains the flexible glycine-rich stretch believed to be involved in substrate binding and/or product release in soluble ScMPP-α (Taylor et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation.

claim: The cryoEM map shows weak density for VrMPP-α residues 340–344, consistent with conformational flexibility.
source: Consistent with this conformational flexibility, our cryoEM map shows weak density for VrMPP-α residues 340–344.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: VrMPP-α/β's sequences are more similar to the yeast (and bovine) soluble MPP subunits than to the respective CIII2 subunits.
source: VrMPP-α/β's sequences are more similar to the yeast (and bovine) soluble MPP subunits than to the respective CIII2 subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence comparison data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The VrMPP-α/β dimer shows secondary-structure elements that are present in ScMPP-α/β and BtMPP-α/β but not in ScCor1/2.
source: Consistently, the VrMPP-α/β dimer shows secondary-structure elements that are present in ScMPP-α/β and BtMPP-α/β but not in ScCor1/2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Yeast, bovine and mung bean MPP-α fold into six additional helices compared to ScCor2 on the posterior surface of the cavity.
source: For instance, on the posterior surface of the cavity, yeast, bovine and mung bean MPP-α fold into six additional helices compared to ScCor2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons in Figure 3C.

claim: Yeast, bovine and mung bean MPP-α contain an extra strand in the β-sheet underneath the helical bundle.
source: Additionally, they contain an extra strand in the β-sheet underneath this helical bundle (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Some structural features of VrMPP-α and -β appear to be specific to plants.
source: Furthermore, some structural features of VrMPP-α and -β appear to be specific to plants, compared to the available structures (Figure 3C–D, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2, Videos 4–5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons in Figure 3C–D and supplementary materials.

claim: VrMPP-α shows a short two-strand β-sheet on its posterior surface.
source: Firstly, VrMPP-α shows a short two-strand β-sheet on its posterior surface.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 3C.

claim: The extended N-terminus of VrMPP-α wraps over the posterior surface of VrMPP-β in the same CIII monomer.
source: Secondly, the extended N-terminus of VrMPP-α wraps over the posterior surface of VrMPP-β in the same CIII monomer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 3C.

claim: A ~ 50 amino-acid N-terminal extension on VrMPP-β folds into an alpha helix that forms extensive contacts with MPP-α of the same CIII protomer as well as with VrQCR7 of the opposite protomer.
source: Thirdly, a ~ 50 amino-acid N-terminal extension on VrMPP-β folds into an alpha helix that forms extensive contacts with MPP-α of the same CIII protomer as well as with VrQCR7 of the opposite protomer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 3D.

claim: VrUCR1's longer N-terminus forms extensive plant-specific contacts with MPP-β's helical bundle and β-sheet.
source: A further difference in the overall configuration of the VrMPP domain comes from VrUCR1, whose longer N-terminus forms extensive plant-specific contacts with MPP-β's helical bundle and β-sheet (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The additional contacts and secondary-structure elements may serve to stabilize plants' MPP domain.
source: These additional contacts and secondary-structure elements may serve to stabilize plants' MPP domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The plant-specific features strengthen the connection between the VrMPP domain and the rest of VrCIII2.
source: Furthermore, they strengthen the connection between the VrMPP domain and the rest of VrCIII2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: These plant-specific features of the MPP domain could play functional roles in plant CIII2's peptidase activity and, potentially, on the coupling between CIII2's respiratory and non-respiratory functions.
source: These plant-specific features of the MPP domain could play functional roles in plant CIII2's peptidase activity and, potentially, on the coupling between CIII2's respiratory and non-respiratory functions (see Discussion).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a hypothesis based on the structural data.

claim: 3D variability analysis (3DVA) was performed on CIII2 alone using cryoSPARC's built-in algorithm.
source: Given CIII2's known conformational flexibility, for example the essential (Xiao et al., 2000; Obungu et al., 2000; Nett et al., 2000) motion of UCR1's head domain during the Q-cycle, we decided to explore the conformational heterogeneity of our CIII2 particles using cryoSPARC's 3D variability analysis (3DVA) (Punjani and Fleet, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis method.

claim: The 3DVA algorithm uses probabilistic principal component analysis to produce distinct 3D volumes that reveal the sample's conformational heterogeneity as a continuous motion.
source: The 3DVA algorithm uses probabilistic principal component analysis to produce distinct 3D volumes (one per principal component) that reveal the sample's conformational heterogeneity as a continuous motion.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis method, supported by citation.

claim: The conformational heterogeneity of the entire CIII2 was analyzed low-pass filtered at 6 Å.
source: We first analyzed the conformational heterogeneity of the entire CIII2 low-pass filtered at 6 Å.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis approach.

claim: Low-pass filtering at 6 Å allowed for the observation of overall changes at the level of secondary structure.
source: This allowed for the observation of overall changes at the level of secondary structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the rationale for the filtering.

claim: Incorporating data at resolutions higher than 5 Å led to the dominance of high-resolution noise from the lipid-amphipol belt, precluding clear results.
source: Incorporating data at resolutions higher than 5 Å led to the dominance of high-resolution noise (in particular from the lipid-amphipol belt), precluding clear results.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the rationale for the filtering.

claim: The 3DVA analysis at 6 Å revealed the lack of QCR10 in some particles.
source: The analysis at 6 Å revealed the lack of QCR10 in some particles, as well as a change in QCR9 (principal components 0–1, Videos 6–7), indicating that these subunits only have partial occupancy in the complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 3DVA data in Videos 6–7.

claim: The 3DVA analysis revealed a change in QCR9, indicating that these subunits only have partial occupancy in the complex.
source: The analysis at 6 Å revealed the lack of QCR10 in some particles, as well as a change in QCR9 (principal components 0–1, Videos 6–7), indicating that these subunits only have partial occupancy in the complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 3DVA data in Videos 6–7.

claim: QCR10 was previously found missing in preparations of mammalian CIII2, likely due to de-lipidation during purification.
source: QCR10 was previously found missing in preparations of mammalian CIII2, likely due to de-lipidation during purification (Letts et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: 3DVA revealed that CIII2 exhibits coordinated 'breathing' motions within and between the protomers of the dimer.
source: More importantly, 3DVA revealed that CIII2 exhibits coordinated 'breathing' motions within and between the protomers of the dimer (components 0–3, Figure 4A–B, Videos 6–9).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 3DVA data in Figure 4A–B and Videos 6–9.

claim: The motions may be parallel or anti-parallel across the dimer.
source: The motions, which may be parallel or anti-parallel across the dimer (compare Videos 6–8 with Video 9), extend from the top of matrix-exposed MPP domain to the bottom of the IMS-exposed regions of CYC1, UCR1, and QCR6.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 3DVA data in Videos 6–9.

claim: The motions extend from the top of matrix-exposed MPP domain to the bottom of the IMS-exposed regions of CYC1, UCR1, and QCR6.
source: The motions, which may be parallel or anti-parallel across the dimer (compare Videos 6–8 with Video 9), extend from the top of matrix-exposed MPP domain to the bottom of the IMS-exposed regions of CYC1, UCR1, and QCR6.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 3DVA data in Figure 4A–B and Videos 6–9.

claim: This finding contrasts with previous assumptions on CIII2's potential for long-range conformational coupling.
source: This finding contrasts with previous assumptions on CIII2's potential for long-range conformational coupling and has implications for the potential interplay between plant CIII2's respiratory and peptide-processing functions (see Discussion).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the 3DVA findings.

claim: The conformational heterogeneity of the UCR1 head domain was examined by using a mask around the IMS-exposed domains of CIII2 at 5 Å.
source: We then examined the conformational heterogeneity of the UCR1 head domain by using a mask around the IMS-exposed domains of CIII2 at 5 Å.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis approach.

claim: The largest variability component revealed a near-continuous conformational motion in the position of the head domain of UCR1, demonstrating its swinging motion from the proximal b position to its distal c position during the Q-cycle.
source: The largest variability component revealed a near-continuous conformational motion in the position of the head domain of UCR1, demonstrating its swinging motion from the proximal b position (close to COB's QP-site) to its distal c position (close to CYC1) during the Q-cycle (Xia et al., 2013; Cooley, 2013; Berry and Huang, 2011; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 3DVA data in Figure 4C and citations.

claim: The motions of the UCR1 head domains of the CIII dimer in this variability component were anti-parallel: when one domain is in the proximal position, the other one is in the distal position and vice versa.
source: Moreover, the motions of the UCR1 head domains of the CIII dimer in this variability component were anti-parallel: that is, when one domain is in the proximal position, the other one is in the distal position and vice versa (Figure 4C, Video 10).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 3DVA data in Figure 4C and Video 10.

claim: Weaker variability components suggested that the position of UCR1 head domains may also be equivalent in some instances.
source: However, weaker variability components also suggested that the position of UCR1 head domains may also be equivalent in some instances.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on 3DVA analysis.

claim: A homology model of the UCR1 head domain was rigid-body fit into the extreme locations of the 3DVA volume and confirmed these corresponded to the Q-cycle proximal and distal positions.

source: Differences in VrCOX5b (shorter N-terminus), VrCOX7a (longer N-terminus with additional contacts to VrCOX3) and VrCOX7c (different path for the unstructured N-terminus) compared to their mammalian counterparts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) are also likely related to the fact that these subunits provide SC-interface contacts in mammals not observed in plants.

claim: Direct contacts between CIII2 and CIV in the plant supercomplex occur in one site in the matrix side and one site in the IMS.

Direct contacts between the complexes occur in one site in the matrix side and one site in the IMS (Figure 8).

claim: Site 1 (matrix side) shows a single hydrophobic contact between one residue of VrQCR8 (Pro31) and one residue of VrCOX2 (Trp59).
source: Site 1 (matrix side), shows a single hydrophobic contact between one residue of VrQCR8 (Pro31) and one residue of VrCOX2 (Trp59) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 8B.

source: The limited matrix-side contacts in V. radiata are in stark contrast to the supercomplex interface in S. cerevisiae, where binding is dominated by interactions between ScCor1 (VrMPP-β) and ScCOX5a (VrCox4) on the matrix side. Instead, V. radiata's site 2 (IMS side) provides the bulk of the protein-protein interactions of the supercomplex, with a hydrophobic interaction between VrQCR6 and VrCOX5c (Leu26 and Leu51 respectively) as well as an interface between VrQCR6 (Pro19 and Lys20) and VrCOX4 (Arg114-Phe117) (Figure 8C).

evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the stoichiometry data.

evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation.

source: Under these conditions, the formation of SC III2+IV in the plant mitochondrion would provide a kinetic advantage to electron flow between CIII2 and CIV by reducing the distance between them relative to CIII2 and CIV freely diffusing in the plane of the membrane.
